reader.summary: The week in the United Kingdom was shaped by a culture clash, a high-profile trial, and a budget season lifted by surprise growth. Sally Rooney's novels were pulled from UK bookstores after her publisher withdrew them over her public support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group the government had designated a terrorist organisation. Comedian Russell Brand's sexual-assault trial opened in a UK court, with prosecutors branding him a ruthless sexual predator and his lead accuser testifying that she knew he raped her. Economically, the UK unexpectedly grew 0.1 per cent in August, a result analysts credited to AI-driven productivity and a shift away from fossil fuels, giving Chancellor Rachel Healey a welcome lift before her autumn Budget, in which she is expected to raise bank taxes and expand the tax net to online marketplaces. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle made their first joint public engagement since settling back in the UK, an event that felt, by all accounts, like a royal appearance. Diplomatically, London sent additional Storm Shadow missiles to Ukraine and hosted President Zelensky in what the PM called a dark moment for Kyiv. Reform UK councillors were caught on hidden camera making racist remarks, deepening the party's credibility problems ahead of local politics.

display.eli5:
Next week in Britain is going to be dominated by two big stories. First, the Russell Brand trial is going to be in the middle of its most dramatic phase, with lawyers questioning witnesses in front of a jury. Second, the Chancellor is going to present her tax plans in Parliament, including raising taxes on banks and taxing online marketplaces.

The Brand trial is big because the prosecution is calling him a sexual predator, and the accuser has already told the jury she knows he raped her. The Budget matters because the bank tax will make London bankers nervous, and the IMF has already told the government that it is not the best idea.

The Sally Rooney book story will also stay in the headlines because the police are looking into a social media post made by the PM's own adviser's wife, and politicians are going to argue about whether pulling her books from shelves was too harsh. The Harry and Meghan story, though, will probably disappear from the news after a few days since it was a one-time event.

A real surprise would be the government formally blocking the Sky-ITV merger, which would start a legal fight and shake up the TV industry. Nobody is expecting that to happen this specific week, but the government has already said it is minded to intervene.
